articles.title: Rate Limiting Like Gandalf: Building a Distributed Cache with Redis
articles.excerpt: The Quest Begins (The "Why") Ever had your API melt down because a sudden traffic spike hammered every endpoint at once? I remember a late‑night deploy where our “simple” in‑process counter crashed un…
articles.body: The Quest Begins (The "Why") Ever had your API melt down because a sudden traffic spike hammered every endpoint at once? I remember a late‑night deploy where our “simple” in‑process counter crashed under a flash sale, and the pager started singing like a busted karaoke machine. We needed a way to throttle requests without turning every service into a bottleneck or rewriting the whole stack. The problem boiled down to: how do we share a counter across many instances, keep it fast, and survive node failures? A naïve approach—each service keeps its own local counter—fails the moment you scale beyond one node. A centralized DB works but adds latency that kills throughput. Enter Redis: an in‑memory key‑value store that can be replicated, clustered, and accessed with sub‑millisecond latency.

articles.title: Red-Teaming a Kids' AI Tutor: How a One-Word Variant Slipped Past Our Prompt-Injection Filter
articles.excerpt: Adversarial testing of the input/output guardrails in Learna Tutor, a TK–8 AI tutoring app. October 2026. Learna Tutor is in private beta. The guardrail module (app/lib/safety.ts) and its test suite a…
articles.body: Adversarial testing of the input/output guardrails in Learna Tutor, a TK–8 AI tutoring app. October 2026. Why this matters Learna Tutor lets children ages ~4–13 chat directly with an AI tutor. That makes safety load-bearing in a way it isn't for adult tools: the users are kids, the failure modes include prompt injection ("ignore your instructions and…"), privacy extraction ("tell me your email"), and academic-integrity bypasses ("just give me the answer"). We needed guardrails we could actually verify, not just a system prompt and hope. The architecture: defense in depth Safety in Learna is three layers, and the tests target the two deterministic ones: Input filter (checkTutorInput) — runs before any model call.

articles.title: VACUUM FULL Locks Your Table the Whole Time. Postgres 19's REPACK CONCURRENTLY Doesn't
articles.excerpt: Book: Database Playbook Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship wi…
articles.body: Book: Database Playbook Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub You deleted 80% of a 200-million-row table and the disk didn't notice. Autovacuum ran. The file stayed the same size. The built-in way to hand that space back has been VACUUM FULL (or its sibling CLUSTER ). It takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and holds it for the entire rewrite, so every read and write on the table waits until it's done. That exact scenario is what depesz ran against the PostgreSQL 19 development branch in April: 200 million rows, 80% deleted, then repack (verbose, analyze, concurrently) .

articles.body: If you opened a personal Google Play developer account after November 13, 2023, you can't publish to production until you've run a closed test with at least 12 testers who stay opted in for 14 days in a row. Then you apply for production access and Google reviews it. I run TestFi, a small testing marketplace, and a lot of what we do now is exactly this. Since May we've run more than a hundred of these closed tests for other developers. This is what I'd tell a friend who just hit the "Your app requires more testing to access Google Play production" screen. The rule, in plain words At least 12 testers, opted in to a closed testing track. 14 consecutive days, counted per tester. After that you apply for production access.

articles.title: Astronomers discover the 1st ever green star, a cosmic zombie just in time for Halloween
articles.excerpt: Imagine if the sun could take on a spooky green glow for Halloween. Scientists have discovered that our star may go green if it turns into a cosmic zombie after its death in billions of years.
articles.body: How awesome would it be if the sun could take on a spooky green glow for Halloween? It turns out that scientists have discovered that our star may indeed go green, but only billions of years from now after its death — and only if it then starts eating planets like a cosmic zombie. That's possible because scientists have discovered that white dwarfs, the type of stellar remnants sun-sized stars leave behind when they die, can actually take on a range of colors including green if they snack on their rocky planets like cosmic cannibals. For stellar scientists, the colors of stars have always been indicative of their temperatures. Cool stars look orange, while stars like the sun look white , and the hottest stars glow pale blue.

articles.body: On Oct. 15, 1997, NASA launched the Cassini spacecraft on a mission to explore Saturn and its moons. It lifted off aboard a Titan 4B rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. It took almost seven years for the Cassini spacecraft to reach Saturn , with the spacecraft entering orbit around the ringed planet in 2004. Another smaller spacecraft called Huygens hitched a ride with Cassini, and it landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005. Cassini spent 13 years studying the Saturn system up close, and the mission lasted about 20 years before coming to an epic grand finale on Sept. 15, 2017 . articles.title: Watch SpaceX launch classified mission for the US Space Force today
articles.excerpt: SpaceX will launch a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California this evening (Oct. 15), and you can watch the action live.
articles.body: SpaceX will launch a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force this evening (Oct. 15), and you can watch the action live. A Falcon 9 rocket is scheduled to lift off from Vandenberg Space Force Base today, on California's beautiful but frequently fog-blanketed central coast, during a four-hour window that opens at 7:44 p.m. EDT (2344 GMT; 4:44 p.m. local time). You can watch it live via a SpaceX webcast , which is expected to begin about 10 minutes before launch. This evening's launch will kick off the USSF-481 mission, which will deliver mysterious payloads to an undisclosed location in the final frontier. Don't expect SpaceX to provide more info during the webcast.

articles.title: Vaonis unveils Atlas, the world's 1st modular smart telescope system
articles.excerpt: Pre-orders are now open for the Atlas, the new modular smart telescope from Vaonis which allows observation with two optical tubes.
articles.body: Vaonis has just announced its new generation of smart telescope technology, known as Atlas. Less of a single smart telescope and more of a new optical system, Atlas was designed with interchangeability and adaptability in mind. Its new SkyDock system allows two optical tubes to be connected and the telescope has live night sky monitoring to predict available observations. You can preorder the Vaonis Atlas with a single Atlas 80 module for $3,990, or $5,490 for the twin at Adorama . But it'll also soon be available at B&H and other retailers. Currently, there is only one optical tube, the Atlas 80, but Vaonis is planning to release add-on modules designed for looking at different night sky objects, including for planetary observation.
